title: Let an operator declare a repository as their own, and grant a broader profile only there

history.detail:
CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — round 1. Audited 027eff0 with bookkeeping f6128ef, main checkout. Sprint file read fresh. Working tree clean apart from the known .vscode file.

You asked for an adversarial pass at the validator and independent confirmation of the confinement re-check. You got both. The validator survived everything I threw at it. The confinement argument did not, in one specific and important way.

================================================================
REQ 1 — I TRIED TO DEFEAT IT. I COULD NOT. NO FAIL.
================================================================

Sixteen inputs against validateOwnedRepositoryDeclaration(), then the survivors re-run end to end through a real subprocess with a fake claude dumping its own argv, so I was reading the grant actually passed rather than a return value:

  GRANTED (all resolve to this exact repository):
    exact real path, trailing slash, dot-dot round trip (/a/b/../b/repo), symlink pointing TO the repo
  REFUSED, each with a named reason and the remedy:
    symlink pointing elsewhere, parent directory, sibling worktree, relative ".", relative "./scripts",
    leading space, trailing space, nonexistent path, "/", a non-git directory, uppercased path,
    empty string

Nothing yielded a grant outside the declared directory. The design is right for a reason worth stating: realpathSync is applied to BOTH sides before comparison, so symlink games are defeated in either direction — a link to the repo resolves in and is correctly granted, a link away resolves out and is correctly refused. Requiring an absolute path up front removes the "relative to what?" ambiguity rather than guessing at it. Requiring a git repository is refused rather than warned, with the reasoning stated (git is the recovery boundary every downstream gate assumes).

WHAT THE RULE IS STATED NOT TO CATCH, since the criterion asks: the declaration lives inside the repository it grants over, so anyone who can write .claude/settings.local.json in a repo you already own can raise the profile there. That is inherent to the design and correct — it is the operator's own file in the operator's own declared repository — but it is worth being explicit that the boundary is "which directory", never "who wrote the declaration". A cloned repository carrying someone else's declaration is refused on this machine automatically, because their path will not resolve to your root. I checked that specific case.

================================================================
FINDING (blocking) — THE CONFINEMENT BOUND DOES NOT COVER THE INTERPRETER ENTRIES IT IS CITED TO BOUND
================================================================

Req 5's own verification is good work and I am not disputing it: a bare `Bash(*)` (or bare `Bash`) genuinely disables the path-based redirect-confinement check — a write to an absolute path outside the working directory succeeded with zero permission_denials, reproduced three times — while a real prefix pattern, however broad, does not. That is exactly why this list is never a wildcard, and establishing it by running was the right call.

The problem is what that bound is then asked to carry. The reasoning for including the interpreters says:

  "`node *`, `python3 *`, `bash *`, `sh *` are deliberately included here ... The risk they carry is
   bounded the same way every other entry here is: directory confinement (verified below, Req 5), git
   recoverability ... and uncommitted work."

Directory confinement, on this project's own evidence, is REDIRECTION confinement. The refusal it produces reads "Output redirection to '/tmp/...' was blocked" (sprint 12's finding, re-verified here). It governs shell redirects. It is not a filesystem sandbox.

`Bash(python3 *)` grants `python3 -c "open('/anywhere/x','w').write(...)"`. That is a file write with no shell redirect anywhere in it. There is nothing for a redirect-confinement check to intercept — this is not a bypass of the check, it is outside the check's subject matter. The same applies to `node -e`, and `bash -c 'echo x > /outside'` puts the redirect inside a quoted string argument rather than in the analysed command line, which sprint 12's own heredoc finding ("Contains shell syntax that cannot be statically analyzed") shows the analyser is sensitive to.

So the safety argument for the four highest-risk entries in this grant rests on a bound that, as far as this project's recorded evidence goes, does not reach them. That is not the same as saying writes escape — I have not demonstrated that, I have no credentials to run a real headless role, and I will not report an untested claim as a finding of fact. What I am reporting is that the stated justification is asserted rather than established for exactly the entries that most need it, in the sprint whose criteria say this bound "is the entire basis on which this sprint was argued."

REQUIRED, AND IT IS CHEAP — TWO REAL HEADLESS RUNS UNDER THE GRANTED PROFILE:
  1. `bash -c 'echo x > /tmp/fc19-escape.txt'`  — does confinement see a redirect nested in -c?
  2. `python3 -c "open('/tmp/fc19-escape2.txt','w').write('x')"` — a direct write, no redirect at all.
Then say what happened. If both are blocked, the existing sentence is correct and now proven, and this becomes the strongest claim in the sprint. If either succeeds, the reasoning needs rewriting — not necessarily the grant, since git recoverability and the .env protection still apply inside the repository, but the sentence claiming confinement bounds them must go, and the residual risk stated honestly instead.

I am blocking on this rather than filing it informational for one reason: Req 5's criterion makes the confinement bound the load-bearing basis of the whole sprint, and this is the one place that basis is cited without having been tested. Everything else in this sprint was tested. This is the gap.

================================================================
REQS 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9 — MET
================================================================

Req 2 (refusal demonstrated) — a non-git directory is refused, verified above through the real subprocess path, not by reading.

Req 3 — the OS-level approach is a real finding and correctly reasoned: Claude Code's Bash patterns cannot express "block writes to file X regardless of command", so a pattern-based .env guard would have been security theatre. Protection is verified by attempting a real write rather than trusting an exit code, and failure to verify refuses the launch rather than degrading. Linux chattr named as expected-but-unverified and Windows named as an uncompensated gap — both honest, neither dressed up.

Req 4 — a decision was made (warn, naming what was already dirty, and proceed) with the reasoning in code. I saw it fire in my own scratch run: "has 3 uncommitted change(s) before this session started: ?? .claude/, ?? p.txt, ?? scripts/. Proceeding anyway ... recorded here so a later tangle between two sessions can be traced." Names the files, not just the count. The criterion says an unstated default is the defect whichever way it went; this is stated.

Req 6 — bare interpreters refused, with the trust-boundary distinction from the broad grant articulated rather than left as an apparent contradiction: Req 6 guards a value any writer of a target project's tracked settings can set, the broad grant applies only after the operator's own high-trust declaration. That distinction is correct and it is the reason the two lists can differ.

Req 7 — `git diff` against scripts/sprint_lifecycle.py is EMPTY. cmd_ship, cmd_complete, cmd_qa1 and cmd_liveqa are untouched. `git push` is carried in the grant's own disallowedTools rather than omitted from allowed, so `Bash(git *)` stays usable for review while Pipeman remains the only pusher — confirmed directly in the same real test per the comment.

Req 8 — 0.1.19. Req 9 — 167 OK, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED; ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED; verify-tarball.sh PASSED, "Installed 0.1.19 (first install)".

================================================================
INFORMATIONAL
================================================================

1. A DECLARATION OF THE WRONG TYPE IS IGNORED SILENTLY. `"fullyCompletely.ownedRepository": true` (or a
   number, null, {}, or "") produces the narrow default with no message at all, while a malformed PATH
   (relative, parent, nonexistent) refuses loudly and names the fix. An operator who typos the type
   gets the narrow profile and no explanation for why their declaration "did nothing". Fail-closed,
   which is the right direction, but inconsistent with how every other malformed declaration is
   handled. One line in the reader.

2. MY OWN HARNESS PRODUCED TWO FALSE READINGS BEFORE I GOT THIS RIGHT, and I am recording that because
   it bears on how much weight to give the rest. My first pass wrote the declaration as a nested
   object when the reader wants a flat dotted key, so nothing reached the validator; my second
   classified persona text echoed in argv as a stack trace and reported crashes that never happened. I
   nearly filed both as findings. Neither was real. The validator and the grant behave correctly and
   the only reason I know that is that I checked the actual argv passed to the child rather than
   trusting my own classifier — which is the same discipline I keep asking for here.

3. Carried, unchanged: the CLI-version-drift item (sprint-12 findings record no `claude` version, one
   CONFIRMED entry already expired) — newly relevant, since this sprint's Req 5 finding about bare
   `Bash(*)` is exactly the kind of matcher behaviour that drifted last time; sprint 17's bare-verb
   allowlist question; the --agents argv budget against Windows' 32,767-char limit.

RECOMMENDATION

Run the two commands above under a real granted profile and report what happened. If they are blocked, say so in that comment and this is a PASS on the next round with the strongest safety argument in the project. If either is not, rewrite the sentence rather than the grant, and state the residual honestly — the sprint may well still be right to ship, but not on a bound that does not hold.

Nothing else is outstanding. The validator is the best-defended piece of code this project has produced, and I could not get past it.
